RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the latest on a number of key injured Red Sox players. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
Ahead of the Boston Red Sox series opener at Tropicana Field against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, interim manager Chad Tracy met with the media and provided updates on a number of injured Red Sox players.
Here's what you need to know:
All eyes were on the All-Star first baseman after Thursday night's win over the Texas Rangers. Contreras exited the game in the eighth inning after being hit by a pitch on the right-hand. According to MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, Contreras told reporters after the game that the injury "felt" like a fracture. While initial X-Rays were negative, as the team learned with infielder Curtis Mead, that doesn't mean Contreras was completely out of the woods yet. According to MLB.com's Ian Browne, the team is waiting for swelling in the 34-year-old's hand to subside before testing his grip strength to determine if additional testing is needed.
Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.
Crochet threw a 30-pitch up-and-down bullpen session on Tuesday back at Fenway Park, representing the most labor-intensive of the four throwing sessions the 27-year-old has done since restarting a throwing progression Aug. 3. According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to carry the momentum from Thursday's come-from-behind win into the final road series of the year against the Rays. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) will get the start for the Red Sox opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for the Rays. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.

Alec Gamboa, who played for the Lotte Giants in the KBO League last year. He failed to re-sign with Lotte, but a year later he debuted in the major leagues and is aiming to make the postseason roster.
On the 18th (Korean time) at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, in the game against the Texas Rangers, Gamboa came in with one out in the eighth inning and no runners on, recorded 2/3 of an inning, allowed one hit and no runs, and earned a hold. It was his second hold of the season.
That day Gamboa entered the game after Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the top of the eighth to put them up 4-3. Starter Sonny Gray pitched well with 6 1/3 innings, three hits (one home run), three walks, six strikeouts and three runs, and second pitcher Wyatt Alls recorded one inning, one strikeout and no runs.
Gamboa came in to face a left-handed batting lineup of Corey Seager and Josh Young. He gave up a single to the first batter, Seager, to right field. Later, he fell behind Josh Young 3-1 in the count but induced a shortstop grounder with a low 95.6-mph sinker, producing a double play to end the inning.
After recording his first hold in his debut by getting Lee Jung-hoo and others out in the Aug. 22 game against the San Francisco Giants, he recorded his second hold of the season. Gamboa's season performance is excellent. In 19 appearances he pitched 29 2/3 innings with 1 win, 2 holds, 1 save, a 1.21 ERA, a .216 batting average against and a 1.04 WHIP.
That day closer Aroldis Chapman could not take the mound because of trapezius muscle stiffness, and another lefty in the high-leverage group, Eric Miller, had earlier shown instability on the 17th against Texas by allowing three runs on 22 pitches in one inning. As a result, rookie right-hander Wyatt Alls and left-hander Gamboa had to take on the high-leverage roles, and setup man Garrett Whitlock had to assume the closer role. All of them then held the one-run lead.
Acting manager Chad Tracy praised Alls and Gamboa's high-leverage performances, saying, "They were really great. They were inserted suddenly into important situations. At times they had to take the mound with the lead, and they did really well."
Gamboa once again successfully passed a high-leverage test for the high-leverage group. Now the question is whether he can join Boston's postseason journey. Boston has a 83-70 record and sits second in the wild-card standings. They are five games ahead of the third-place Cleveland Guardians, so barring an upset they are all but certain to secure the 5 seed.
Over the Monster, which reports on Boston news, listed Gamboa in the "pitchers who need to prove themselves" spot while predicting the postseason roster. The outlet said, "He is a player who had a pleasantly surprising performance this year. He even made two starts as an opener. In recent weeks the bullpen has had injuries, and combined with his own performance, he has risen to the point of being used in higher-stakes, high-leverage situations."
Closers Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Eric Miller, Tyrone Guerrero and Garrett Crochet are confirmed. It is likely that one more left-handed reliever will be added and the rest filled with right-handers.
They went on to say, "If Aroldis Chapman, Eric Miller and Garrett Crochet are the confirmed left-handed bullpen pieces, the final left-handed spot could be a competition between Hobani Moran and Gamboa," and added, "If I had to pick the final four now, I would choose Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Moran and Gamboa," predicting they would make the postseason roster.
Boston regional outlet MassLive also highlighted the performances of Gamboa and Alls on the 17th, saying, "He seized an unexpected opportunity this year, expanded his standing, and his entry into the postseason roster race—which would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago—is worthy of high praise," introducing that Gamboa has performed well enough to be included on the postseason roster.
Gamboa was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the ninth round, 281st overall, in the 2019 draft. But he couldn't break through the Dodgers' deep minor league system, and last year he joined the KBO League's Lotte Giants as a replacement player and delivered a sensational performance.
He had an especially strong performance, including being named player of the month for June, but fatigue accumulated late in the season and elbow pain caused him to miss several turns in the rotation, preventing a smooth finish. His KBO League stats were 19 games, 108 innings, 7 wins, 8 losses and a 3.58 ERA.
Although Gamboa failed to re-sign with Lotte, he said of going to Lotte, "It was a good opportunity to show myself elsewhere. I wanted to experience a bigger and new environment than Triple-A in the U.S. I believed I would show good pitching there, return to the U.S. and seize another opportunity," and added, "Before going to Korea I had never been abroad. Experiencing another country, seeing how polite the people there are and how much they love baseball, and seeing what style of baseball they play was really fun," saying it was an opportunity that lifted his spirits.
Was failing to re-sign with Lotte a blessing in disguise? After signing a minor league deal with Boston he made an emotional big league debut and now stands on the verge of making the postseason roster. Gamboa is becoming a symbol of a life turnaround.

The good news is that Tracy said it's getting better. The Red Sox have Garrett Whitlock, who is more than capable of closing games, and some more bullpen reinforcements potentially on the way. However, Chapman has been one of the most dominant closers in baseball throughout his career, especially in Boston.
Chapman was the American League Reliever of the Year last year, posting a 1.17 ERA in 67 games. This year, he has a 1.95 ERA in 52 games and has 34 saves. The Red Sox's duo of him and Whitlock figures to be very important in October, but the 38-year-old needs to be healthy for that.
"Obviously, you guys know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment. So we'll just monitor it day to day," Tracy said.

The New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox seem destined for another October clash. You can smell the narrative building now. The Red Sox will be painted as the underdogs due to their horrid start to the season. Fine. Whatever makes them feel better.
For the Yankees, this could be a tipping point, a chance to regain that sense of dominance over their hated rival. To that end, New York might have just gotten a piece of news that could further tip the scales in its favor, and it has to do old "friend" Aroldis Chapman.
After dropping the first two games of their series against the Texas Rangers, Boston mounted a late-inning comeback following a Trevor Story three-run homer in the eighth inning against Texas's all-world closer Jacob Latz. Coming out to secure the victory in the ninth wasn't Chapman, though; instead, it was another former Yankee, Garrett Whitlock. After the game, it was revealed that Chapman was "unavailable" because he's dealing with a sore lat.
Red Sox interim manager said that it's an issue that Chapman has been dealing with for a few days, and that the team will be conservative with his usage for the time being. The 38-year-old, who recently learned the importance of throwing strikes, has seen his command get spotty over his last two outings, issuing three walks in the process. Perhaps the injury is to blame?
Red Sox injury issues, including Aroldis Chapman, Willson Contreras, and others, could give Yankees the upper hand
At this point, it's unclear whether or not Chapman will need to head to the IL, but either way him being less than 100% bodes well for the Yankees. That will be especially true if he remains active and reverts to his wild ways in the upcoming playoff matchup.
Chapman isn't the only Boston player banged up, either. Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on the hand during the Red Sox's win over the Rangers. X-rays were initially negative, but the former St. Louis Cardinal said he's suffered hand fractures before and that this felt the same way. He'll be sent for imaging and further tests to determine the true extent.
Contreras has been hit a total of 24 times this season, the third-most in baseball. He seems frustrated, too, saying that it will keep happening "if nobody does anything about it." Sounds like he's frustrated that Boston pitchers haven't come to his defense, threatening to cause an issue for the Red Sox even if his hand injury proves to be nothing serious.
That's not the end of the problems for the Red Sox. Roman Anthony, who missed nearly four months due to a torn finger ligament, is slumping hard. After an initial burst in his first two games back after being activated on August 30, Anthony has slashed just .200/.268/.338 thus far in September.
The biggest news of all, though, is Chapman. If he avoids the IL but is diminished, it could give the Yankees a key advantage in the most crucial moments of the expected matchup. The Sox's other primary bullpen lefty, Erik Miller, is also suffering from mechanical issues at a particularly brutal time. Capitalizing on that edge will be a must, and if the Red Sox fall to New York due to a Chapman postseason meltdown, the moment will be that much sweeter.

Red Sox news: Aroldis Chapman dealing with concerning injury with playoffs approaching appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
In signature 2026 Boston Red Sox fashion, they rallied late and completed a comeback from three runs down against the Texas Rangers after they scored three runs in the eighth to take a 4-3 lead they would not relinquish. But even with the Red Sox facing a save situation in the bottom of the ninth, it wasn't closer Aroldis Chapman who came off the bullpen to shut the door on the Rangers.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy rolled with Garrett Whitlock in the bottom of the ninth, and Whitlock responded with a save, improving Boston to 83-70 on the season. After the game, Tracy revealed that Chapman wasn't available on the night anyway as the hard-throwing lefty is currently dealing with a "lat issue", as per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe.
Tracy added that the Red Sox are going to be "conservative" with utilizing Chapman off the pen to end the regular season, as keeping him healthy for the postseason is going to be important for this team.

Chapman last made an appearance for the Red Sox on the 13th of September in a 4-1 win over the Kansas City Royals. While he did allow two walks in that save situation, he made up for it by striking the side, making it look as though he wasn't dealing with any injury.
Nonetheless, the Red Sox, now armed with a seven-game cushion over the AL Wild Card cutoff line, have the luxury anyway to bring Chapman along slowly.
The Red Sox also have other injury matters to deal with. According to Healey, Tracy also said that first baseman Willson Contreras, who recently returned to the lineup (returning on September 13 against the Royals), is dealing with a bruised right hand and is currently day-to-day. The good news for Boston is that his X-rays turned out negative.
With the Red Sox on the cusp of sealing a postseason spot, they can afford to do whatever it takes to keep their core players healthy so that they can trot out their best squad come postseason time.

ARLINGTON -- Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman was unavailable to pitch in Boston’s 4-3 win over the Rangers on Thursday at Globe Life Field due to lat tightness and is considered day to day.
“We're going to be conservative with [it],” interim manager Chad Tracy said postgame. “It's getting better, but we're going to make sure it gets there. That's why he wasn't available tonight.”
According to Tracy, Chapman has been dealing with the tightness for the last couple of days, so the team will continue to evaluate him.
“Obviously, you guys know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment. So we'll just monitor it day to day,” Tracy said.
On Thursday, Garrett Whitlock came in to close out the game, getting a groundout to first, issuing a walk and inducing a 6-4-3 double play to end it.
“[Whitlock is] great,” Tracy said. “He's reliable. He's done it before. If Chappie's down, he's very reliable in any spot we put him in.”
Through 51 games, Chapman owns a 1.95 ERA and a 1.14 WHIP, with hitters batting .190 against him. His 34 saves are tied for third in the AL and tied for fifth in the Majors. He is MLB’s all-time leader in relief strikeouts with 1,399.
Chapman’s absence Thursday was the latest injury concern for a Red Sox team that has had to rely on its depth throughout the season, with eight pitchers currently on the IL. Despite the injuries, Chapman has been impressed by the way younger players have responded when given opportunities.

This is why we watch! Trevor Story's season looked dead and buried both three months and three weeks ago. He's battled injury, surgery, rehab, way too many strikeouts, and growing chatter from knuckleheads like me who have repeatedly questioned if he even belongs back in this lineup.
Well tonight, he came to the plate with the Sox down 3-1 in the eighth and on the verge of getting swept. He was facing a tough reliever in Jacob Latz, a Texas team that was 63-1 when leading after seven innings, and the weight of his team going a combined 0-17 with runners in scoring position in the series up to that point.
Then he did this:
As somebody that's been leading the "Trevor Story is cooked " charges, I love this so much! Nothing can humble and amaze quite like baseball, and after months of hard work, grinding behind the scenes, and having to deal with all the noise, Story smashed a 108mph line drive home run not only in the face of Latz and Texas' playoff hopes, but also in the face of all those who have been doubting him for weeks (hand raised).
It's just one game, and the real test doesn't start until the 29th, but boy did this have to feel incredible for Story who hadn't gone deep since May 13th. To do it in that moment, in his home town, and against the backdrop of everything that's happened this year is just so perfectly baseball. It's why we love this game so much, and why people like Story are willing to put in the work behind the scenes for months on end to get the chance to do something amazing like that.
I know some of you might not believe it after what I've written about him in recent weeks, but I truly am very happy for Story! He deserves all the credit tonight!
Oh, and in addition to Story's game changing three-run homer, he followed that up by starting double plays on defense to end both the eighth and ninth:
Baseball really is the best!
Studs
Trevor Story: If I didn't put him here, I'd have to legally resign from Over The Monster.
Wilyer Abreu: He looked a little better tonight with a sharp single in the fourth and a walk that turned into a run on Story's three-run shot.
The bullpen: The comeback wouldn't be complete without the pen holding it down, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable with lat tightness, Wyatt Olds, Alec Gamboa, and Garrett Whitlock combined to go 2.2 scoreless innings.
Duds
Only one dud tonight, and that's me given my recent stance on Story's playing time. The crow is delicious, and I hope it remains on the menu well into October!
One other important note
Just before Story's home run, Willson Contreras was hit in the hand by a pitch and had to leave the game. The good news is x-rays were negative, but given x-rays were also negative after Curtis Mead got hit in July, I'm not going to be celebrating this one until we get further confirmation.
X-rays were negative on Willson Contreras, at least initially, but he remains sore.
Aroldis Chapman was unavailable due to lat tightness and is day-to-day.
Willson Contreras: "Sore. Painful. My hand was numb for like five minutes. That was the reason I came out of the game. I have fractured, before, the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it’s not a fracture on the top of the bone. I’m just frustrated."

Trevor Story hit a three-run homer in the eighth inning as the Boston Red Sox overcame a three-run deficit to defeat the Texas Rangers 4-3 on Thursday in Arlington, Texas.
Story’s blast came against Texas closer Jacob Latz (3-3) and erased a 3-1 deficit.
The victory allowed Boston (83-70) to avoid being swept in the three-game series and ended the Rangers’ four-game winning streak. Josh Jung hit a solo home run for Texas (76-77), which fell a game behind the Houston Astros (77-76) at the top of the American League West.
Wyatt Olds (2-0) earned the win by tossing one scoreless inning. Boston starter Sonny Gray allowed three runs on three hits in 6 1/3 innings. He struck out six and walked three.
Texas had the tying run on first with one out in the ninth, but Garrett Whitlock got Jake Burger to ground into a game-ending double play for his fourth save.
Danny Jansen had two of the Rangers’ four hits, including an RBI single.
Boston’s Willson Contreras left the game after he was hit by a pitch on his right hand in the eighth inning. Contreras leads the Red Sox with 27 home runs.
Jung hit a solo shot in the first inning to open the scoring. It was his 10th homer of the season.
Texas extended its lead to 3-0 in the third. After two walks and a sacrifice bunt, Jansen singled home Wyatt Langford, and Burger scored on Evan Carter’s sacrifice bunt.

The Boston offense struggled in the first two games of the series. The Red Sox struck out 15 times as the Rangers won 4-2 on Tuesday, and the visitors were held to three hits in a 7-3 loss on Wednesday.

Latz (3-3) entered after Wilyer Abreu walked starting the eighth and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch from Jakob Junis.

Roman Anthony hit into a run-scoring forceout in the seventh.

Trevor Story Saves Red Sox From Crushing Sweep With One Swing originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
For seven innings, the Boston Red Sox appeared headed toward a disastrous conclusion to their stay in Texas.
Trevor Story changed everything with one swing.
Story crushed a three-run home run in the eighth inning Thursday night, lifting Boston to a dramatic 4-3 victory over the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field. The comeback allowed the Red Sox to avoid a three-game sweep and improve to 83-70. Boston entered the seventh inning without a run and trailed 3-0. The Red Sox had managed only three hits through six innings and continued to waste the few scoring opportunities they generated.
Then the game suddenly flipped.
The Red Sox pushed across their first run in the seventh when Nate Eaton scored on a throwing error by Rangers second baseman Nicky Lopez. That cut the deficit to 3-1, but Boston still needed a much bigger response.
Story supplied it one inning later.
Trevor Story Delivers Red Sox's Biggest Swing
Wilyer Abreu opened the eighth with a single before Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch. Isiah Kiner-Falefa entered as a pinch runner, placing two runners aboard with one out.
Story then hammered Jacob Latz's offering 394 feet to left-center field.
The three-run blast turned a 3-1 deficit into a 4-3 advantage. It was Story's fourth home run of the season and accounted for three of Boston's four runs.
Story finished 2-for-4 and produced the Red Sox's only hit in seven at-bats with runners in scoring position. Boston recorded only five hits all night, making Story's timely power even more important.
The late rally rewarded starter Sonny Gray for keeping Boston close after a difficult beginning.
Texas scored once in the first inning on Josh Jung's solo home run before adding two more in the second. Gray settled down from there and held the Rangers scoreless over his final 4 1/3 innings. The veteran right-hander allowed three runs on three hits over 6 1/3 innings. He struck out six and walked three while throwing 102 pitches.
Red Sox Bullpen Protects One-Run Lead
Wyatt Olds recorded the final two outs of the seventh and returned for a scoreless eighth, earning his second victory of the season. Angel Gamboa completed the eighth before Garrett Whitlock handled the ninth. Whitlock issued a walk but did not allow a hit, securing his fourth save.
Boston's defense also turned two double plays, helping its pitching staff hold Texas to four hits.
The victory did not erase the disappointment of losing the first two games of the series. Texas still won the set after taking Monday's opener 4-2 and Tuesday's game 7-3.
It did, however, keep a frustrating trip from becoming a sweep at a critical point in the season.
For most of Thursday night, the Red Sox looked lifeless. Story needed only one pitch to completely rewrite the ending.

item.content:encoded:
This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox starter is working his way back from a right elbow injury.
Video Transcript
What's up, everyone?
Zach Coe here for Roundtable.
Ahead of Tuesday night's loss to the Rangers, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters that reliever Justin Slayton's season was over after an orthopedic visit revealed degenerative changes in his flexor mass, which required a PRP injection, effectively ending his season.
So obviously, the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in baseball, backend of Aroldis Chapman, Justin Slayton, and Tayron Guerrero when he returns from the injured list.
But the loss of Slayton is still a really big one for this Red Sox bullpen, especially in the postseason when managers tend to be more aggressive with the hooks on both starters and relievers.
It was a pretty underwhelming season for Slayton when you look at the final line.
It was a 4.60 ERA in 31 1/3 innings.
But he was prone to a couple blowup starts, and that really inflated his ERA for much of the season.
It'll be interesting to see how Tracy's able to piece together the bullpen in Slayton's absence.
Of course, like I said, you have the backend pretty solidified with Tayron Guerrero handling the seventh, Garrett Whitlock in the eighth to All-Star Aroldis Chapman, who's been one of the best closers in baseball over the last two seasons.
But it's how you get to them that I really have some concerns about, and there are plenty of guys that are available to fill that role, but it's whether or not they'll be able to capitalize on their opportunities.
First one being Greg Weiser.
I wrote about it a little bit earlier, but ever since he was recalled from his brief demotion to Triple-A, he's been incredible for the Red Sox, stepping up as they lost guys like Whitlock to an IL stint, Slayton, who landed on the IL shortly after Whitlock, and most recently Guerrero.
There's also Tanner Houk, who's working his way back from Tommy John surgery he underwent last year.
He's gonna try to make a return in a bullpen capacity for the last week of the season.
And then there's the big wild card of it all in Garrett Crochet, who continues to throw side sessions as he tries to get back in a relief role for the postseason.
He's been on the injured list since April 29th with left shoulder inflammation.
So any of those guys are more than capable of stepping up and filling that role.
It's just gonna be about whether or not they're, one, healthy enough to go out there and throw on a near nightly basis like the team might need them to in the postseason, and two, whether or not they're gonna be productive enough.
Obviously, with Houk, he's coming back from Tommy John surgery, and typically you see guys be a little bit wild with their control when they first come back from Tommy John.
We saw it in Houk's first relea-- We saw it in his first rehab appearance with Portland.
He walked two guys, and a run scored as a result.
But it's been a little bit better, since then in the two appearances following that.
So we'll see if that is something that he can shake.
And then Crochet, he's just We haven't seen him in so long, it's tough to say whether or not he's gonna be as effective as he once was.
And even if he isn't able to get to the 2025 Cy Young runner-up caliber, can he at least give you enough to kind of bridge that gap between the starter and to the backend of your bullpen?
And then there's kind of a wild card in it all, and a bit of a forgotten man in Johan Oviedo, who obviously has electric stuff, but he's made only one appearance in a Red Sox uniform before landing on the IL with right elbow inflammation.
So he's planning on making a rehab appearance with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday night, and then they'll figure out the next steps with him.
But Red Sox have plenty of options to fill that void left behind by Slayton.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

Garett Crochet wants to pitch in the postseason without making a single rehab appearance. That’s audacious enough, but how about playing in the postseason, without having ever played in the big leagues at all? That could be the situation Braiden Ward finds himself in. If you need to refresh your memory, Ward was the little speedster who was running wild all over Grapefruit League diamonds this spring. He hasn’t gotten a chance to show whether he can do that in the Majors yet, but Chad Tracy isn’t ruling it out. “Every time he gets on, he’s not afraid,” Tracy said. “That’s the thing. If he gets on base, he’s looking to go. That’s a unique trait. There’s a lot of guys who can run and steal bases and then there’s other guys who are, every single time they get on, almost regardless of the timing.” (Conor Ryan, Boston.com)
But a lack of speed on the base paths isn’t really the Red Sox problem right now as they muddle through a middling September. Strikeouts are. “The Red Sox are swinging and missing too much and not walking enough. This month, they have the eighth-most strikeouts and seventh-fewest walks. That doesn’t play in the postseason. Making contact does.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
After he initially returned to the big leagues with a bang, Roman Anthony is one of the Sox hitters who’s struggling to make contact right now. But he doesn’t sound worried. “I’m right where I want to be,” said Anthony. “I came back with enough time to get a good number of plate appearances, and to fail like I am right now and to succeed like I did in the beginning, and then kind of meet in the middle and continue to grind out every single day and get ready for what we want to be a long postseason run. [The playoffs are] what you play for after such a long year … At the end of the day, those few weeks are the only thing that really matters.” (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
Unfortunately, the other big power threat in the Sox lineup is also struggling to get back up to speed. Willson Contreras homered last night, but he’s still dealing with a nagging hamstring injury. “I ran pretty good there on the ground ball to shortstop, but I need to manage my leg better,” he said. “I know it’s feeling good and it’s feeling alright, but on a hard-hit ball like that, I know I’m going to be out. I was just trying to put pressure on him, see if he made a bad throw or whatever. Next time, I’ll manage better.” (Chris Cotillo, MassLive)
With Anthony and Contreras struggling in different ways, it’s important to remember that this team’s success has been built on depth, not individual star power. “Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.” (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
Fortunately, the Sox have some depth in the good guy department, too. After the departure of Liam Hendriks, who had been nominated for the Clemente Award seven times throughout his career for his charitable efforts, Garrett Whitlock has stepped in and picked up the baton. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)

When Erik Miller on September 16 took the mound in front of the Texas Rangers, it didn't take long for things to go awry. Miller's command has never been perfect, but something was definitely off in Arlington, Texas.
It took only three pitches for the big lefty to plunk Corey Seager, and he walked Jake Burger two batters later. On his lone pitch to Brandon Nimmo, the former New York Met knocked a game-changing RBI double to center field, and things crumbled from there.
Ezequiel Duran's two-RBI single, which gave the Rangers a three-run lead, was the last at-bat of the inning before Miller was spared by Adley Rutschman catching Duran stealing. The outing was Miller's worst since he joined the Boston Red Sox at the trade deadline — he allowed three runs on two hits, a walk and a hit batter with one strikeout.
The outing against the Rangers was the second one in as many games that has given Miller trouble. On September 13 against the Kansas City Royals, Miller lasted just a third of an inning after conceding two walks and a fielder's choice. Garrett Whitlock entered after him and gave up a single, but the Royals' lone run of the game was charged to Miller.
Red Sox need Erik Miller to right recent command issues as soon as possible to be right for postseason
After his appearance in Texas, Miller made a concerning statement about his recent struggles. It could be a disastrous sign for Boston's October bullpen.
"Kinda working through some stuff right now," Miller said. "There's some stuff I'm trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. I mean, at some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. I had been doing really well and there are some bad habits I'm kinda falling back into so, yeah, just gotta work through it, gotta get back to what I was doing and go from there."
Miller has been one of Boston's biggest relief weapons since the trade deadline. The Red Sox need him in his best shape all the more with Tyron Guerrero on the injured list and after the announcement that Justin Slaten's season has ended.
Before his shaky command popped up, Miller had done a solid job at limiting free passes, one of the major concerns from his tenure with the Giants. Over his 12 outings in August (including one with the Giants) Miller allowed three walks and a hit batter (0.943 WHIP). Through five outings in September, he's up to six walks and a hit batter (2.077 WHIP). The combination of fatigue and decreased command will make for a brutal outcome for Boston.
Thankfully, the Red Sox are expecting some relief reinforcements for the playoff run. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working toward returns in long relief. But having them plus prime Miller would be the best outcome.
The Red Sox must work more closely with Miller to address his mechanical issue, whatever it is. Over his last two outings, he's served up damaging pitches or free passes, and that won't get Boston far in October, especially given the fatigue its rotation has been showing.

Whitlock reflects on 'real honor' of Clemente Award nomination
This story was excerpted from Ian Browne's Red Sox Beat newsletter. To read the full newsletter, click here. And subscribe to get it regularly in your inbox.
When it comes to his many charitable endeavors, Red Sox right-hander Garrett Whitlock is the ultimate example of someone who throws himself in with passion and never seeks recognition for them.
So when it was announced on Tuesday that Whitlock is Boston’s nominee for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award -- the highest recognition for philanthropy a baseball player can get -- it was an honor he took in with great appreciation.
And that’s because of who Clemente was and his ever-lasting legacy.
For that reason, Whitlock is thankful for former manager Alex Cora’s decision to take the Red Sox to the Roberto Clemente Museum on Aug. 18, 2022, prior to a game against the Pirates.
Often when players get nominated for the Roberto Clemente Award, they are compelled to really dig into who the late Hall of Famer was and all that he represented.
Fortunately for Whitlock, thanks to that museum visit four years ago, he already feels well-versed in what made Clemente a legendary human.
“When we went to Pittsburgh, [Cora] got a group of us and we went to the Roberto Clemente Museum. It was super cool and they had a very in-depth tour guide and everything like that,” said Whitlock. “It was really neat learning all about him and his history, and then also the history of the award, because they do a really good job there, explaining all that.”
Clemente died in 1972 in a plane crash when he was, fittingly, embarking on a humanitarian effort of delivering relief supplies to Nicaragua, which had just been hit with a devastating hurricane.
“I got to know about everything he did off the field, and obviously the tragic accident of the airplane, and why he was on that airplane, so I was really grateful to get to know all that,” Whitlock said. “And then obviously having AC as a manager, who is of Puerto Rican descent, I got to know exactly how much Clemente meant to Puerto Ricans. It's been really neat to see the award winners throughout the years and everything, and now it's a real honor to be nominated for it.”
The Roberto Clemente Award is given annually to the Major League Baseball player who best represents the game through character, community involvement, philanthropy and contributions on and off the field.
In Clemente, Whitlock feels like he has a kindred spirit.
“He really exemplified what it means to not put baseball [above all else]," Whitlock said. “And I think that that's something that I try to live by every day, is knowing that, ‘Hey, this is a job and this is a game. This isn't what life is all about.’ I think he exemplified that the most in just saying there are infinitely more important things than this game. He did that to the utmost level, so it's really neat that they honored him for that and they have a specific award meant to say, ‘There’s a lot more to this game.’”
Whitlock has displayed that mentality his entire career, which started in 2021, when he had a role model in Nathan Eovaldi, who showed the younger players what it meant to embrace community efforts.
Not that Whitlock needed much convincing. It is just in his personality.
Whitlock has a chance to be the third Red Sox player to win the Roberto Clemente Award, after Tim Wakefield (2010) and David Ortiz (2011) went back to back.
It is an honor that would be so fitting for Whitlock, who feels that giving back is every bit as important to him as getting those key outs in the eighth inning.
Being a baseball player serves as the ultimate platform for Whitlock’s message to carry weight.
The most visible of Whitlock’s charity work is in his role as Red Sox captain for the cancer-fighting Jimmy Fund.
This browser does not support the video element.
But there is so much else he does that the public doesn’t see. Forget about his relief pitching statistics, which are impressive enough in their own right. This is the one that matters most to him: He annually ranks among the team’s leaders in community appearances.
It is common for Whitlock to put his sponsorship funding toward a teammate’s charitable program rather than building his own brand.
This season alone, Whitlock has supported the Jimmy Fund and Dana-Farber, Boston Children’s Hospital, the Red Sox Foundation, Massachusetts General Hospital's Home Base Program, Pro Athletes Outreach, One Church Boston, Highlands Church, the CPP One Foundation and the Chantel Guardians Syndrome Foundation, and has provided direct financial assistance for a family's IVF treatments.
Perhaps most poignantly, Whitlock sponsored the wish of a young boy from Georgia who suffered a traumatic brain injury, allowing him and his family to experience Fenway Park for the first time earlier this season and fulfill his dream of throwing out a ceremonial first pitch.
Of that effort, a member of the Red Sox community relations staff wrote the following as part of his nomination: “It is emblematic of Garrett’s approach to philanthropy: personal, thoughtful, and centered on people rather than recognition.”

Good morning! Last night, Jake Bennett was unable to hold the Rangers in check during the team's 7-3 loss in Texas. Some of his numbers look good (seven strikeouts against just one walk), but he also surrendered eight hits in just 4.2 innings, which did in his evening.
With just ten games left in the season, the question now becomes how should the Sox use Bennett going forward? With some combination of Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez likely to get lined up in a best of three Wild Card Series, do you just hold Bennett on the sidelines and hope he gets to come back into the fold as a fourth starter in the ALDS or even ALCS? Or do you start transitioning him to some sort of relief role?
It's a bit of an awkward moment for Bennett. He's been getting knocked around during his last two outings while Suarez is seemingly getting locked in. It almost certainly cuts him out of the Wild Card rotation, and if the Sox get some combination of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Tyron Guerrero back to add to Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller in the bullpen, Bennett largely gets squeezed out of relevance.
So how do you want him used? Do those six shutout innings Bennett threw against the Yankees back on August 29th make you want the Sox to find a role for him if they play New York? Do you think he's just a young pitcher who looks out of gas and want to hide him until the team needs a fourth starter?
Use this space to talk about Bennett and the rest of the difficult upcoming pitching staff decisions, and, as always, be good to one another.

When the Boston Red Sox sent former top-prospect Marcelo Mayer to the San Francisco Giants for Erik Miller, CBO Craig Breslow was sending a major signal. This season is about winning, and Miller will be more help with that now.
For a while, the hard-throwing lefty has been exactly that. A major spark out of the bullpen who makes the Red Sox incredibly intimidating on the mound in the late innings. In his first 14 appearances with Boston, Miller gave up just two runs.
The last two games have been more of a struggle for Miller, though. In 1.1 innings, he’s given up four runs. That includes three runs in Wednesday’s rough loss to the Texas Rangers, which was good enough for Miller to earn a loss.
Boston Red Sox RP Erik Miller Opened Up on Struggles
Following Wednesday’s loss, Erik Miller faced the media following the game. There, he explained that his main issue on Wednesday was that he had control issues. Those control issues put him in bad counts, which made him predictable.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well,” Erik Miller said. “Just not getting ahead of guys. Getting behind. Falling into hitters’ counts… Guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end well. Just kind of working through some stuff right now.”
Red Sox fans and media both noticed Miller saying that he’s working through some stuff. Luckily, that doesn’t mean an injury. It’s more a reference to letting his mechanics get away from him.
“Yeah. Some stuff I’m trying to clean up a little. At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. You’ve been doing really well and some bad habits kind of come up. So, I’ve just got to work through it. Get back to what I was doing and go from there,” Miller said.
The Red Sox need the version of Miller they’ve largely gotten since the trade. He has a 2.87 ERA in Boston, to go along with a 1.277 WHIP and 14.9 strikeouts per nine. That’s in 15.2 innings over 16 appearances.
Garrett Crochet Will Return to the Red Sox as a Reliever
The Red Sox bullpen is set to get a major boost soon. Ace pitcher Garrett Crochet is getting ready to make his return, but it won’t be as a starter. It’ll be as another power lefty for the bullpen to use.
The expectation had been that Crochet won’t be able to make a rehab and would jump back in right as the first-round of the playoffs start. That may not be the case now. It was recently reported that he could be ready even sooner. That means he’ll potentially pitch in the regular season as a kind of rehab.
“The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason,” Chris Cotillo of MassLive wrote. “It’s not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what’s effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings.”
It’s excellent news for the Red Sox. With Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, a healthy Garrett Crochet, and Erik Miller, Boston can feel very confident if they get just five innings from a starter.

For the last two seasons, Garrett Whitlock has been one of the best pitchers the Boston Red Sox's bullpen has to offer. But the righty has considered changing that.
Whitlock told Tim Healey of The Boston Globe that he would consider a return to life as a starting pitcher (subscription required). Whitlock in 2021 debuted with Boston as a reliever, but he began starting some games shortly after in 2022. He made four starts in 2024 and planned to take his full season as a starter, but a UCL injury derailed that plan.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to," Whitlock said, via Healey. "So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Some fans and people in the Red Sox organization could be excited to hear Whitlock say he's interested in reprising his role as a starting pitcher. Boston has just one righty starter in its rotation this year, Sonny Gray, and he'll be a free agent at the end of the season, barring an unexpected contract extension. Whitlock's success in the bullpen could translate to more in the rotation and he could compete for Gray's former spot.
Red Sox should keep Garrett Whitlock in bullpen despite his willingness to return to a starting role
But Whitlock's history as a starter isn't as clean as it is from the bullpen. Whitlock went on the injured list twice in the 2022-23 seasons with hip and elbow issues. He missed all but four appearances of the 2024 season after he underwent the internal brace procedure to repair his UCL. His elbow even flared up after a period of heavy use out of the bullpen this season. Adding starts into his repertoire hasn't worked before, and though it could work now since Whitlock said he's more in-tune with his body, it isn't a risk the Sox should be willing to take.
Whitlock has had more success as a reliever than as a starter, though he's pitched far more in relief and the sample sizes are far from equal. The veteran has posted a 4.29 ERA over 109 innings across 23 appearances as a starter and a 2.37 ERA over 254.1 frames in relief. The Red Sox need right-handed rotation depth, but they also have Tanner Houck, Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo recovering from injury, and none of them have established themselves in another role as seamlessly as Whitlock has.
Whitock told Healey that he would return to a starting role if the Red Sox want him to (he's under team control until after the 2028 season due to two club options) or if any new team he signs with wants him to change. For now and in 2027, the Red Sox should stick with the good thing they have, which is Whitlock as one of the most dangerous relievers in the league.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe disscusses the reemergence of Greg Weissert as a reliable relief option for the Red Sox bullpen.Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After a historic July that saw the Boston Red Sox use high-leverage arms on a near-nightly basis, one of baseball's best bullpens became injury-ravaged, losing Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Justin Slaten to fatigue-related injuries. The losses of Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero forced interim manager Chad Tracy to turn to other relievers in high-leverage spots. Among those arms is right-hander Greg Weissert, who, after a brief trip to Triple-A Worcester, has come up huge for the bullpen.
In his first 48 appearances of the season, Weissert posted a 3.97 ERA in 45.1 innings pitched. The 31-year-old right-hander struggled in particular when taking over in situations with men already on base, allowing 13 of 29 inherited runners to score, which, at the time, was the third-most among all relievers.
After needing 34 pitches to get through an inning in Boston's 13-inning marathon win over the Chicago White Sox on Aug. 6, Weissert fell victim to the numbers game, getting optioned to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7 in favor of a fresher arm. However, it wound up being just a six-day trip as he was recalled on Aug. 13 when the team placed Whitlock on the IL.
In 12 appearances since being recalled, Weissert has more than made up for the losses of Whitlock, who returned on Aug. 29, Guerrero, who is slated to return ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas and Slaten. He's allowed only two earned runs on 11 hits, striking out 13 and walking only four in 10.2 innings of work. Most importantly, Weissert has performed much better when entering 'dirty' innings, allowing only one of seven inherited runners to score.
Despite Whitlock's return and Guerrero's imminent return, Weissert's reemergence as a reliable option will help in the final 11 games of the regular season and the postseason run, as Tracy announced Tuesday that Slaten will not return in 2026 after undergoing a PRP injection in his right elbow to treat degenerative changes in his flexor mass.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener against the Texas Rangers, the Red Sox will look to even up the series in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

Ranger Suarez tossed his second straight seven-inning start and the Boston Red Sox scored in their final three at-bats en route to a 5-1 win over the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon.
Suarez (7-4) struck out eight, scattered five hits and allowed one run while completing his seven frames in 96 pitches as Boston (81-68) snapped its three-game losing streak.
Roman Anthony, Adley Rutschman and Nick Sogard each had multiple hits while Wilyer Abreu hit a two-run double that gave the Red Sox a sixth-inning lead they would not relinquish.
Carter Jensen’s 24th home run of the season marked the only scoring for Kansas City (66-83), which opened the series with a win Friday.
The Red Sox took the lead with two runs on three straight hits in the sixth. After Mickey Gasper and Rutschman knocked back-to-back singles to right to chase Royals starter Randy Dobnak (3-4), Abreu drove them home with a two-out double to deep center off reliever Anthony Gose.
The lead grew in each of the next two frames, beginning with Sogard hitting a leadoff double and scoring on Caleb Durbin’s RBI single off the Green Monster in the seventh.
After Garrett Whitlock struck out the side in the Royals’ eighth, Trevor Story and Sogard posted back-to-back doubles to plate another run.
Aroldis Chapman followed with a scoreless ninth to tab Suarez with the victory.
The teams plowed through three scoreless innings with just one baserunner: Bobby Witt Jr.’s one-out single in Kansas City’s opening frame. Suarez stranded him on third after recording back-to-back outs, including an inning-ending strikeout of Vinnie Pasquantino.
Suarez retired the Royals 1-2-3 on 10 pitches in the second and third innings while Dobnak faced the minimum, striking out three batters through the first third of the game.
In the fourth, Anthony turned a leadoff single through the right side into the opening run. After moving to second on Gasper’s grounder, Anthony scored when Rutschman knocked a single into center.
After finishing the fourth around Pasquantino’s two-out double, Suarez retired five straight before Jensen’s one-out solo homer inside Pesky’s Pole in the sixth. The southpaw stranded runners in the next two frames, including back-to-back strikeouts to cap the seventh.
–Field Level Media

The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May.
But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games.
After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to throw off the mound again.
Now that he’s been able to do so three times, and is scheduled for a fourth bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, there is legitimate hope he can be on the roster when the Red Sox open their postseason on Sept. 29 -- likely at Yankee Stadium.
This time, assuming he makes it back, Crochet will be cast in a much different role, but one that can still be impactful.
Figuring you have questions about how and when Crochet fits in, here are some answers.
Can Crochet make it back before the regular season ends?
It’s not impossible. His next key step after graduating from bullpen sessions will be to face hitters. That could happen as soon as this weekend, depending on what the club decides after Tuesday’s session.
Ideally, when it comes to Crochet’s situation, the Triple-A season would go a little longer. But, alas, it ends on Sunday.
It seems more likely Crochet will throw live batting practice and/or some type of simulated game rather than getting into a Minor League game, perhaps doing so multiple times.
Would this leave time for one tune-up before the regular season ends on Sept. 27? Perhaps, but not necessarily.
Would Crochet be thrown right into the fire of the playoffs?
What if there isn’t time for Crochet to pitch in any type of game setting before the Wild Card Series starts? Would the Red Sox still put him on the roster?
Well, if he’s throwing up to his capabilities, the answer is absolutely yes.
“It's Garrett Crochet,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “If Garrett Crochet looks like Garrett Crochet and he's healthy and able to go out there and pitch, and it looks like him? Yeah, that helps any team.”
What would Boston’s bullpen cast look like with Crochet in the mix?
In a word, dominant. Through their first 150 games of the season entering Tuesday, Boston’s bullpen has a 3.11 ERA, best in the Majors. That’s without Crochet.
Now, add Crochet and possibly 2024 Tanner Houck, who is on a Minor League rehab assignment in his return from Tommy John surgery, and Tracy’s relief crew could have a succession of pitchers with nasty stuff.
At 38 years old, lefty Aroldis Chapman continues to be a force. He has one of the best eighth-inning setup men in the game in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. Tyron Guerrero, the righty with triple-digit heat, is due back in the next couple of days after missing the last couple of weeks with right shoulder inflammation. Power lefty Erik Miller has been tremendous since he was acquired at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline.
Brayan Bello, who hasn’t had much success has a starter this season but has been largely stellar in relief, is another weapon. Add Crochet and Houck to those five pitchers and the Sox would have bullpen depth that would be the envy of most teams.
How would the Sox use Crochet?
The beauty of Crochet is that he could work out of a hybrid role, meaning he could be available for whichever part of the game Tracy needs him most.
Keep in mind that Crochet was a relief pitcher not just in college at Tennessee, but also for the White Sox before being converted to a starting role in ‘24. He has experience working in the early, middle and late part of games.
Thinking outside the box, the Sox could even deploy Crochet as an opener if the occasion called for it, given his experience starting games.
“He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said. "He pitched out of the 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that, too."

ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.
